note: Shared by both editions. Unicode behaviour recorded here is specified in the standard and stable. Printer-specific values are vendor-dependent and carry todo_verify.

editions.en: Implementer-facing. Bidi algorithm, shaping, code pages, raster rendering. Path in doc_en.
editions.zh: Shop-owner-facing. How to recognise a bad sample print and what to ask a vendor before paying. Written separately, not a translation. Path in doc_zh.

source_types.official-authority: Published or administered by a named body, including standards bodies where identified.
source_types.public-regulation: Derives from published law, decree or regulation.
source_types.unverified: Not attributable to either of the above as written. Treat as unknown.

mandatory_ligatures.name: lam-alef
mandatory_ligatures.note: Not stylistic. The unligated sequence is wrong.

combining_marks_zero_width.note: Counted by string length but occupy no printer column. Cause of column drift on real supplier data.

mirrored_characters.note: Mirror once. Doing it in both the renderer and application code cancels out.

base_direction_must_be_explicit_per_line.note: The first-strong default takes paragraph direction from the first strongly directional character, so an item name beginning with a Latin brand or SKU lays out mirrored relative to surrounding lines.

known_failure_modes: numeric separators detach from the number and jump to the opposite end of the run
signs and percent marks migrate to the wrong side
a line's base direction flips when the name starts with Latin text
padding computed on code point count instead of display width

control_characters.name: RLM
control_characters.use: invisible strong RTL; pins a neutral run

bidirectional.storage_rule: store logical order, render visual order, never store visual order

forms.name: Western (ASCII)
forms.note: Widely used on printed commercial documents across the Arab world.

forms.name: Arabic-Indic
forms.note: Used in parts of the region.

forms.name: Eastern Arabic-Indic
forms.note: Persian/Urdu context; distinct glyphs for some digits.

rules: make the digit form a template setting, not a code branch
convert at render time only, never in stored data
never mix forms on one document
switching digit form does not change ordering behaviour, only glyphs

options: printer firmware with an Arabic ROM font
shaping_owner.note: Per-model fact, not discoverable at runtime. Wrong assumption prints disconnected isolated letters.

code_pages.name: CP864
code_pages.note: DOS Arabic. Contains presentation forms, so text must be pre-shaped.

code_pages.name: CP720
code_pages.note: DOS Arabic, transparent ASMO. Different layout from CP864.

code_pages.name: Windows-1256
code_pages.note: Covers the base repertoire; expects the renderer to shape.

code_pages.name: ISO-8859-6
code_pages.note: Base Arabic, limited repertoire, uncommon in POS firmware.

code_page_numbers_omitted_deliberately.reason: Vendors renumber the code page table and clone firmware diverges from documented ordering while claiming compatibility. Read the value from the target printer's command reference and confirm by printing.

single_byte_pages_insufficient_for_mixed.note: Arabic plus a Latin brand name plus a currency symbol on one line exceeds any single-byte page.

costs: printer font and size commands no longer apply
resolution must match printer dot density

currency_glyph_coverage.note: ROM fonts lag Unicode by years. Where coverage is uncertain print the ISO code instead of the symbol.

amount_column_side.value: conventionally mirrored from LTR layouts: description at the right edge, amount at the left
amount_column_side.note: Consistency between header, item lines, totals block and tax breakdown matters more than the choice itself.

paper_width_guidance.note: Stack the name on its own line with the amount beneath it.

line_breaking.truncation_note: Cutting a word changes the final letter's positional form, producing a different misspelled word rather than an obviously clipped string.

qualifications.note: French is widely used in retail documentation in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, often alongside Arabic on the same document, making mixed-direction layout the normal case.
Arabic and English routinely appear on the same receipt. Some markets may have expectations about the language of tax figures.

deployment_pattern.note: Only the print template drives the rendering concerns in this file.

acceptance_test_requires_native_reader.note: Disconnected letters, a flipped line direction and column drift all look plausible to a reviewer who does not read the script.

script.name: Hebrew
script.shaping_note: Non-cursive. Letters do not join, there are no positional forms and no presentation-forms block is involved. This is the principal contrast with Arabic.

final_forms.mechanism: separate codepoints chosen at spelling time, not glyph variants selected by a renderer
final_forms.note: Because a final form can only occur at the end of a word, and the end of a word is at the left of the printed run, its position is a reliable reversal detector usable by someone who does not read Hebrew.
final_forms.affects_search: A substring search using the regular form will not match the final form. Normalise search input, not stored data.

combining_marks_zero_width.name: nikud (vowel points) and cantillation marks
combining_marks_zero_width.note: Absent from ordinary commercial text but arrive through copied supplier data, causing the same column drift as Arabic harakat.

mirrored_characters.note: Mirror once. Doing it in both the renderer and application code cancels out.

base_direction_must_be_explicit_per_line.note: Same requirement as Arabic. Israeli catalogues carry Latin brand names routinely, so a name-initial Latin run is an everyday case rather than an edge case.

known_failure_modes: the whole string is reversed because visual and logical order were confused
numeric separators detach from the number and jump to the opposite end of the run
signs and percent marks migrate to the wrong side
a line's base direction flips when the name starts with Latin text
padding computed on code point count instead of display width
bidirectional.storage_rule: store logical order, render visual order, never store visual order

byte_order.note: Hebrew legacy encodings disagree about whether bytes are in reading order or printing order. The two are not distinguishable from the bytes themselves — ISO-8859-8 and ISO-8859-8-I are byte-identical and differ only in declared order.
byte_order.failure_mode: Text prints reversed rather than garbled. It still looks like Hebrew, so it survives review by a non-reader.

forms.name: Western (ASCII)
forms.note: The form used on Hebrew commercial documents. There is no Hebrew equivalent of the Arabic-Indic digit choice.

hebrew_letter_numerals.note: Used for Hebrew-calendar dates and traditional enumeration. Treating them as a number format would be a mistake.

rules: no per-market digit-form setting is required, unlike Arabic
digits still form left-to-right runs inside right-to-left text

shaping_owner.note: Hebrew is non-cursive, so the Arabic question of whether firmware or application shapes does not arise.

options: visual order, as CP862-derived firmware modes expect
printer_byte_order.note: Per-model fact, not discoverable at runtime. The most important thing to establish about a Hebrew printer. Sending logical bytes to a visual-order mode prints words backwards; reordering in the application when the firmware also reorders is backwards for the same reason.

code_pages.name: Windows-1255
code_pages.note: Near-superset of ISO-8859-8. Carries the shekel sign at 0xA4 and supports vowel points. Usual modern choice.

code_pages.name: ISO-8859-8
code_pages.note: Position 0xA4 is the generic currency sign, not the shekel.

code_pages.name: ISO-8859-8-I
code_pages.note: Byte-identical to ISO-8859-8; the suffix declares logical order and nothing else.

code_pages.name: CP862
code_pages.note: DOS Hebrew. Stored visually because DOS had no bidi support. Still present in thermal printer firmware.

code_page_numbers_omitted_deliberately.reason: Same reason as Arabic: vendors renumber the code page table and clone firmware diverges from documented ordering while claiming compatibility.

single_byte_pages_insufficient_for_mixed.note: A Hebrew item name beside a Latin brand beside a currency symbol exceeds any single-byte page, and mixed script is the ordinary case in Israeli retail.

recommended_print_path.value: code page is viable; raster conditionally
recommended_print_path.note: Because Hebrew needs no shaping, single-byte code page printing genuinely covers the script. Use raster when the receipt mixes scripts, when the shekel sign must appear, or when the printer's byte order cannot be established.
costs: printer font and size commands no longer apply
resolution must match printer dot density

glyph_coverage.note: Present in Windows-1255, absent from ISO-8859-8. ROM font coverage is a separate question from code page definition. Print the ISO code where coverage is uncertain.

amount_column_side.value: conventionally mirrored from LTR layouts: description at the right edge, amount at the left
amount_column_side.note: Consistency between header, item lines, totals block and tax breakdown matters more than the choice itself.

layout.width_rule: one column per non-combining character; the only correction is for zero-width marks

paper_width_guidance.note: More comfortable than Arabic and far more so than CJK; Hebrew commercial text is compact.
Names carrying an embedded Latin brand need the name stacked on its own line.

line_breaking.truncation_note: Unlike Arabic, truncation does not change any glyph, because Hebrew letters have no positional forms. It is merely ugly.

qualifications.note: Not yet covered by a country file in this repository. Tax, invoicing and receipt-content requirements are undocumented here.
Hebrew usually appears as a secondary language on the document rather than the primary one, making mixed-script handling the whole job.

deployment_pattern.note: Only the print template drives the rendering concerns in this file. Chinese-owned businesses in Israel typically pair a Chinese back office with a Hebrew till and Hebrew receipts, requiring two product name fields.

acceptance_test_requires_native_reader.note: A reversed string still looks like Hebrew. The final-form position test is the one check a non-reader can perform reliably.

width.note: The dominant failure: code measuring with a plain character count under-counts by a factor of two and overflows the line.

ambiguous_width_characters.note: One column in a Western font, two in a CJK font. The printer decides; measure empirically.

line_budget.note: Name must go on its own line; this is the only workable layout, not a degraded one.

rom_font_present.note: Printers sold into Western markets frequently have no CJK font and will print boxes regardless of what is sent. Most common cause of works-on-my-desk failures.

glyph_coverage.note: Rare surname characters, Traditional forms and the shop's own name are where coverage runs out.

simplified_traditional.note: Conversion is not one-to-one; one simplified form can map to several traditional ones. Store two name fields rather than converting at runtime.

languages.deployment_relevance: Chinese is the back-office language across most deployments in this repository, so this file applies to every country in it, not only where Chinese reaches the customer receipt. Customer-facing in Malaysia and on kitchen tickets in Chinese-owned restaurants.

unaffected.note: Latin script with no diacritics in normal commercial use; no code page work needed.

failure_mode.note: Output stays readable when wrong. Pina for Pina-with-tilde, Sao for Sao-with-tilde. Passes review by anyone testing with clean data, unlike Arabic or Thai which fail loudly.

special_cases.note: Not decorative; outside ASCII and often the first thing to break.
i uppercases to I-with-dot, dotless-i uppercases to I. A naive toUpperCase produces a different word.
Conventional fallback SS changes string length and therefore column width.

printing.note: A printer whose code page was never set mangles every accented character. Most common single cause.

euro_sign.note: Select CP858, Windows-1252 or ISO-8859-15, or print EUR.

normalisation.note: Decomposed input loses the accent entirely through a single-byte code page, and inflates character counts so column maths disagrees with printed width.

languages.description_length_vs_english: roughly a fifth longer for es and pt; longer for fr and de, which also produces unbreakable compounds

line_breaking.space_role: separates phrases and sentences, roughly where English uses a comma or full stop
line_breaking.standard: UAX #14, which handles Thai by dictionary lookup rather than character properties alone
line_breaking.note: Wrapping on whitespace breaks inside words, producing a different string rather than a clipped one.

mark_stack.clipping_risk: Tight leading clips upper tone marks. Legible to a non-reader, wrong to a Thai reader.

sara_am.note: Single codepoint rendering as a mark plus a trailing tail; can split across a line break if decomposed.

collation.note: These five vowels are written before the consonant they follow phonetically, so dictionary order files the word under the consonant. Affects product lists and search, not printing.

digits.rule: template setting, never mix forms on one document

calendar.rule: store one canonical form, convert at render time

printing.raster_caveat: Resolves stacking, glyph coverage and code page, but NOT line breaking, which happens upstream.

kitchen_printer_separate_test.note: Frequently a different and cheaper model than front of house.

script.note: Latin script that behaves like a non-Latin one.

d_with_stroke.note: A distinct letter, not a d to be normalised away.

no_single_byte_page_covers_it_fully.note: Including CP1258, the page nominally designed for Vietnamese.

encodings.name: Windows-1258
encodings.problem: Encodes some syllables as base letter plus combining tone mark, so a naive transcode drops or mangles tones even when the page is nominally correct.

encodings.name: TCVN3 (ABC)
encodings.problem: Legacy; splits Vietnamese across two fonts, one lowercase one uppercase.

code_page_selection_is_insufficient.note: Selecting CP1258 is not evidence Vietnamese will print correctly. Print and look.

printing.line_breaking: ordinary whitespace wrapping is correct; unlike Thai, no dictionary needed

supplier_data_risk.note: Catalogues from long-established suppliers frequently arrive in legacy encodings. Import a small batch first and have a Vietnamese reader check it; correcting a corrupted catalogue after prices and stock are attached is expensive.

rules: quality-marked vowels sort after their base vowels

languages.description_length: words are short but numerous, so names wrap across more lines than English; budget two-line item names at 58 mm

script.note: Non-cursive, left to right, whitespace-separated, no stacking marks. The rendering concerns that dominate the Arabic, Thai and CJK files are all absent. The problems are in the data and in code page selection.

homoglyphs.note: A group of Cyrillic letters is visually identical to Latin letters with different codepoints. Strings render and print correctly and compare unequal, so search returns nothing, imports create duplicate records and stock splits across them.
homoglyphs.source_of_entry: keyboard layout switching during manual data entry; the Latin and Cyrillic forms share a physical key
homoglyphs.detection_unit: one whitespace-delimited token, not the whole line; a Cyrillic name beside a Latin brand is ordinary data
rules: validate at entry and at import permanently, not once as a migration
flag for a human, never auto-convert; a mixed-script record may already carry stock movements and sales history
forbid Cyrillic letters, or letters entirely, in article codes and SKU fields

normalisation.note: Through a single-byte code page the combining mark is dropped and the short i becomes plain i, leaving a different but still plausible word rather than a box or a question mark. Also inflates character counts and breaks equality against a composed copy.

yo_folding.note: Russian printed matter routinely substitutes e for io. Both spellings occur in real catalogues.
yo_folding.rule: fold in search input on both sides of the comparison; do not fold stored data

russian.note: The alphabet places io immediately after e, but U+0401 sorts before U+0410 and U+0451 sorts after U+044F, so codepoint order files one at the very top of a product list and the other at the very bottom.

collation.ukrainian: Ghe-with-upturn after Ghe, and Ie, Byelorussian-Ukrainian I and Yi inside the alphabet, while their codepoints U+0490, U+0404, U+0406 and U+0407 sit outside the contiguous run
collation.serbian: Dje, Je, Lje, Nje, Tshe and Dzhe order inside the alphabet, while their codepoints U+0402 to U+040F all fall before U+0410

koi8_byte_order.note: KOI8-R orders its letters in a pseudo-Latin transliteration sequence inherited from teletype practice, so sorting on stored 8-bit bytes from a KOI8 source is wrong in a third way, distinct from codepoint order.

collation.recommended: ICU with the specific locale (ru, uk, sr, bg, kk, mn); a generic Cyrillic collation is not sufficient

no_default_code_page.note: Two live traditions, DOS and Windows, disagree across the whole range above 0x7F. Unlike a CP437 printer facing English, an unconfigured Cyrillic printer is not approximately right; it is either right or completely wrong, and which one is not discoverable at runtime.

code_page_family.note: Per-model fact and the first question for a Cyrillic printer. Settled cheaply by one sample print.

code_pages.name: Windows-1251
code_pages.covers: Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Macedonian

code_pages.name: CP866
code_pages.covers: Russian and Bulgarian fully; Ukrainian partially, carrying Ie and Yi but not Ghe-with-upturn or Byelorussian-Ukrainian I
code_pages.note: The box-drawing block is what makes its mojibake recognisable when Windows-1251 bytes are sent to it.

code_pages.name: CP1125
code_pages.covers: CP866 plus the missing Ukrainian letters

code_pages.name: CP1131
code_pages.covers: CP866 variant carrying Belarusian short u alongside Ukrainian letters

code_pages.name: KOI8-R
code_pages.note: Letters in pseudo-Latin order. Stripping the high bit yields a rough Latin transliteration, which is the design intent and a useful fingerprint.

code_pages.name: ISO-8859-5
code_pages.note: Rare in POS firmware; appears in data feeds.

code_pages.name: Mac Cyrillic
code_pages.note: Rare; turns up in files from older Mac systems.

code_page_numbers_omitted_deliberately.reason: Same reason as Arabic and Hebrew: vendors renumber the code page table and clone firmware diverges from documented ordering while claiming compatibility.

single_byte_pages_insufficient_beyond_sl.note: Kazakhstan standardised an altered Windows-1251 variant (STRK1048) for this reason. For these markets the single-byte path is a dead end rather than a compromise.

recommended_print_path.value: code page is viable for the Slavic set once the family is confirmed; raster beyond it
costs: printer font and size commands no longer apply
resolution must match printer dot density

mojibake_signatures.symptom: box-drawing characters where capitals should be, wrong Cyrillic lowercase, stray numero, currency and square symbols
mojibake_signatures.cause: Windows-1251 bytes into a CP866 printer

mojibake_signatures.symptom: curly quotes, dashes, euro and per-mille where capitals should be
two Latin-ish characters per intended letter
one question mark or blank per letter, ASCII unaffected
mojibake_signatures.cause: transcoded to a page with no Cyrillic; the letters were destroyed at the encoder

mojibake_signatures.symptom: one evenly spaced box per letter
mojibake_signatures.cause: no Cyrillic ROM font; the code page is irrelevant

mojibake_signatures.symptom: correct Russian but wrong or missing Ukrainian or Kazakh letters
mojibake_signatures.cause: right code page family, wrong variant

fiscal_device_may_own_the_receipt.note: Several Cyrillic-script markets are understood to operate mandatory fiscal-device regimes in which the device, not the application, produces the receipt and therefore decides the code page, template and field order. Unresearched.

signs.note: Added in Unicode 7.0 (2014), later than every code page listed above, so it is absent from all of them by construction rather than by chance.
Absent from Unicode 13.0; assume no ROM font carries it.

traditional_abbreviations_still_common.note: Written abbreviations predate the signs, remain common in print, and are encodable in every code page above.

currency.fallback: print the ISO code where the sign cannot be rendered

number_format.note: The group separator is a space character, which is a line-breaking hazard as well as a formatting one. Use a no-break space and confirm it survives the print path.

market_currency_changes.change: euro adopted 2026-01-01 at 1.95583 BGN to 1 EUR; lev ceased to be legal tender 2026-02-01
market_currency_changes.dual_display_period: from 2025-08-08 to 2026-08-08 per secondary reporting, with one source giving 2026-06-30 instead
market_currency_changes.note: Secondary reporting only, not confirmed against the Bulgarian authorities. There is no Bulgaria country file in this repository.

layout.width_rule: one column per character in a Western font context

east_asian_width.narrow_or_neutral: the rest of the Cyrillic block, including Ukrainian, Belarusian, Serbian, Kazakh and Mongolian letters
east_asian_width.note: The Ambiguous set is exactly the 33-letter Russian alphabet. A printer with a CJK-derived ROM font may render those letters at two columns while the letters beside them stay at one, producing mixed widths inside a single word with an entirely correct encoding.

paper_width_guidance.note: Cyrillic retail names run long with no compensating density, unlike CJK. Budget two lines for the name.

line_breaking.truncation_note: Truncation changes no glyph, as in Hebrew; it is merely ugly.

serbian.note: Cyrillic and Latin are both used for the same language and readers use both. Transliteration is close to letter-for-letter but not length-preserving: three Cyrillic letters map to Latin digraphs, so a round trip is not guaranteed.
serbian.rule: store what the customer is meant to see; do not convert silently at print time

localized_letterforms.note: Drawn differently in the Bulgarian and Serbian traditions from the Russian ones, handled in real fonts by language-tagged alternates. A thermal printer ROM font carries one set, normally the Russian shapes. Affects labels and signage rather than receipt legibility.

kazakhstan_latin_transition.note: Timetable has moved more than once. The POS implication does not depend on the date: both scripts will be present in real data for years, the same product will exist under two names, and search has to cross the scripts. Plan for two name fields rather than a conversion.

digraphia.uzbekistan: Latin official, Cyrillic still widely read
digraphia.mongolia: Cyrillic with two letters outside Windows-1251

qualifications.note: None is covered by a country file in this repository. Tax rates, fiscal device requirements, invoicing rules and mandatory receipt content are undocumented here.

deployment_pattern.note: Only the print template drives the code page and width concerns. The homoglyph, normalisation and collation concerns apply to the back office as well, and hardest there, because that is where product data is created. Chinese-owned businesses in these markets typically pair a Chinese back office with a local-language till and local-language receipts; a market in script transition may need three name fields.

acceptance_test_requires_native_reader.note: A dropped breve leaves a different but still plausible word, and a mixed-script product name looks correct to everyone. Two of the tests in the file are data tests rather than print tests, and those are the ones a native reader looking at a sample receipt will pass without noticing.
